proposed_scaled_derivatives_step2_1: 2.1 The coefficient construction in step 1.1 and its Taylor expansion give vector polynomials $R_m$ of degree at most $m$ with $f(t+hc_j,U_j)=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}h^mR_m(c_j)+\delta_j(h)$, where $\max_j\|\delta_j(h)\|=O(h^M)$. Apply componentwise reproduction from [F3] and define $e_h(\tau)=\sum_j\ell_j(\tau)\delta_j(h)$. Then $I_Mg_h(\tau)=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}h^mR_m(\tau)+e_h(\tau)$ and every derivative of $e_h$ through order $M-1$ is $O(h^M)$, because its basis is fixed. Substituting into the DEFINING integral in [F1], rather than identifying a degree-$M$ polynomial from only its $M$ stage values, gives $u_h(\tau)=u+\sum_{s=1}^M h^sP_s(\tau)+R_h(\tau)$ with $P_s(\tau)=\int_0^\tau R_{s-1}(a)\,da$ and $R_h(\tau)=h\int_0^\tau e_h(a)\,da$. These are the same integrated coefficients used in step 1.1 through the row integrals $Q_{ij}$. Thus $\deg P_s\le s$, $P_s(0)=0$, $\|R_h\|_\infty=O(h^{M+1})$, and for $1\le j\le M$, $R_h^{(j)}=h e_h^{(j-1)}=O(h^{M+1})$. Differentiating the expansion annihilates every term with $s<j$ and bounds the remaining terms by $O(h^j)$. Hence $\|u_h^{(j)}\|_\infty=O(h^j)$ for $1\le j\le M$; derivatives above $M$ vanish by the defining integrated cardinal sum. This argument also covers $M=1$ and a node at zero. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]
